title: The trio at the Victoria Cafe: no rehearsals, Pete Brown's playing
summary: The trio never rehearsed; Brown played around melodies; the 105-seat cafe had a tiny dance floor.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Now, with your trio, when you started your trio with Don Frye and Pete Brown, how did you run it as far as getting the tunes together that you wanted to play...? Even though it was a trio, I'm sure that you wanted the tunes expressed a certain way. Did you rehearse with that band, with that trio?

No, we didn't have to do no rehearsing with that band. We had a good piano player, which was Don Frye, one of the top pianists, and a fellow by the name of Pete Brown, a good alto player -- great musicians. Everybody loved the way he played. And we never had no rehearsal. We'd just get on the bandstand, started calling different numbers, and... Don Frye would call the keys out for the saxophone player, you know. Each number, we'd play numbers like... One of our special numbers was "In The Mood." We'd play a lot of Benny Goodman's stuff. We couldn't play so much, because we only had one horn. But what I like about Pete Brown, he'd play... If he didn't know the song so well, didn't know the melody, he would play around the melody after the first or second set, until he got the melody right. He'd always play around that melody.
He was quite an inventive and an expressive musician. And he played a lot of music that was very good for dancing in some of those small groups.

Yeah. He played a lot of dance music. Because we had a little small floor there in the Victoria Cafe. The whole place held about 105 people; it could hold that many. It had a small dance floor, a dance floor that had... It could hold about five or six couples on the floor. Small place. The place was packed every night. Every night.
